title: Soviet Jewry
hookLine: Jews in the Soviet Union are denied the right to practice or to leave

lines: A KITCHEN IN MOSCOW, CURTAINS DRAWN.
cards: Someone keeps an ear on the stairwell. In a kitchen in Moscow, late at night, curtains drawn, a handful of people lean over one worn Hebrew textbook, its pages typed and retyped and passed from hand to hand.
Teaching Hebrew like this could cost a person their job, or worse. Every person at this table has asked the government for permission to leave for Israel, and every one has been told no.
They have a name for themselves: refuseniks.

teach.b: In the Soviet Union, religion was officially discouraged, and Jewish life was squeezed hard. Synagogues were few and watched. Hebrew was difficult to learn.
Jews often met suspicion at universities and at work. And for a long time, few were allowed to leave. Then some Jews began to apply anyway, to emigrate to Israel.

Applications were refused, sometimes with a vague reason about state secrets, and the person who asked could lose their job just for asking. That's a refusenik: someone refused permission to leave. Some waited for years.

Inside, they did what Jews had done under pressure before: learned in secret, taught each other Hebrew, kept the holidays quietly. On Simchat Torah, young Jews gathered outside a Moscow synagogue and danced in the street.
Outside the country, Jews and non-Jews around the world took up their cause, with a slogan from Exodus.

teach.h: LET MY PEOPLE GO, TO HOLD A FEAST.
teach.b: Moses and Aaron stand before Pharaoh and say: "Let My people go, that they may hold a feast unto Me in the wilderness." Notice the second half, the part a slogan can leave off. The demand isn't only to leave.

It's to be free to worship, to hold the feast: freedom to go, and freedom to be who you are where you stand. In time, the gates opened, and families left, some to Israel, some to America and elsewhere.
Tomorrow, one refusenik who found a way to stay free inside a prison cell.

how: Jews retell the story of the refuseniks alongside the Exodus, and 'Let my people go' from Exodus 5:1 became the slogan of the worldwide movement for Soviet Jewry.

games.q: you are a young engineer in Moscow. you applied to leave for Israel, were refused, and lost your job. what do you do?
o: withdraw the application and keep quiet.
teach Hebrew in a friend's kitchen at night.
give up on Jewish life altogether.
games.why: refuseniks learned and taught Hebrew in secret, in private apartments, and kept the holidays quietly.

practice: Think of something you're free to do that someone, somewhere, is not: read a book of your choosing, learn a word of Hebrew, light a candle, say a blessing out loud, sit in silence without anyone checking.
Choose one and do it now, slowly and on purpose, remembering the kitchens where it cost something. If you pray, you can do it as a prayer.

wordCard.voice: Refusenik. A Soviet Jew refused permission to leave, often punished for asking, who kept Jewish life going in secret.
